blogs.description: Introducing Kimi K3.1 Pro Kimi K3.1 Pro landed on the Kimi API today - it's not yet open weights, but Moonshot promise "Full model weights…
blogs.content:
Introducing Kimi K3.1 Pro

Kimi K3.1 Pro landed on the Kimi API today - it's not yet open weights, but Moonshot promise "Full model weights will be released by Nov 4, 2026".

 They're also offering a "Highspeed" version that's 2-3x faster, at twice the price (except for input token cache hits, which are priced the same).

 The US dollar pricing is $2.00/million tokens for input and $10/million for output - the same as GPT-6.1 Sol and half the price of Claude Opus 5.5.

 Moonshot's own benchmarks show Kimi as approximately level with Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra - beating them on a few benchmarks, coming close on others.

 Artificial Analysis scored Kimi at 55 - ahead of Claude Fable 5.1, GPT-6 Astra, and Gemini 4 Argon (all at 53) and behind only Claude Opus 5.5 (58).

 This is the first time a (soon-to-be) open weight model has scored this highly against the frontier.

 I tried it out via the Moonshot API using the llm openai endpoint command I added to LLM 0.32 back in August:

 llm openai endpoint \
 https://api.moonshot.ai/v1 \
 --key kimi \
 -m kimi-k3.1-pro \
 "Generate an SVG of a pelican riding a bicycle" \
 --responses \
 -o reasoning_effort low \
 > kimi-k3.1-pro-pelican-low.stdout.txt \
 2> kimi-k3.1-pro-pelican-low.stderr.txt

 llm openai endpoint can run prompts against any OpenAI-compatible endpoint but doesn't log the results, hence the extra options to save stdout and stderr (the reasoning trace).

 Here are the pelicans I got for Kimi K3.1 Pro on the three reasoning levels it supports - low, medium, and max. This is max:

 For comparison, I ran fresh pelicans against Kimi K3 on those three reasoning levels.

 Via Hacker News

 Tags: ai , generative-ai , llms , llm , llm-pricing , pelican-riding-a-bicycle , llm-release , ai-in-china , moonshot , kimi

blogs.content:
Welcome back to This Week in Stratechery!

 This week marks a new era for Stratechery, which is now presented by Stripe . I’m excited about what this partnership can unlock, starting with in-person on-video episodes of Sharp Tech. Check out the YouTube video above (or watch it on Stratechery ); and, for subscribers, look forward to a bonus episode showing up in your subscriber feed every Sunday morning (add your feed on sharptech.fm ).

 Here were a few of our favorite topics this week:

 The Best iPad; The Worst Phone. John Gruber wrote a great review of the iPhone Duo, which we broke down on Dithering . In short, it’s an iPad that fits in your pocket, and it’s awesome at that; just don’t expect a good phone. Plus, on Monday we discussed Apple’s surprising partnership with Meta for edge AI, a topic I also covered in Tuesday’s Update . — Ben Thompson

 The SS Sarandos in a Storm. The past week has seen a flood of bad news for Netflix: layoffs, executive departures, another disappointing round of earnings, and another hit to a share price that has taken a 40% hit over the past 12 months. Wednesday’s Update provides a comprehensive state of the union , and we doubled back on the topic for a fun conversation on this week’s Sharp Tech , where we divided the company’s problems into areas that can be fixed (the content) and what may be much trickier (growing the business in a world where Meta and YouTube are primary engagement competition). — Andrew Sharp

 You Can See Everything, But Can’t Trust Anyone. Allow me to be the 1,000th person on the internet to recommend Nathan Fielder’s new Elizabeth Holmes documentary, You Can See Everything . After declaring on Sharp Tech last week that I wasn’t interested in seeing it, I did in fact check it out, and wound up loving it. I wrote about my experience on Sharp Text , with 5 spoiler-free notes for anyone still on the fence, and 5 more reactions for anyone who’s seen it. Compulsively watchable (and worth seeing in a theater), I think it may have also been the most effective document of our modern media environment I’ve ever seen. — AS

---

 Presented by

 It’s kind of weird to be the Internet’s number one fan of ads. What makes it even weirder is that I have been the Internet’s number one fan of ads without actually having ads on Stratechery .

 That second part is changing: I’m super excited to announce that Stripe is going to be the presenting sponsor of Stratechery. And, at the end of the day, for me it couldn’t be any other company.

 One of my hangups in terms of advertising is that I take my ethics super seriously, and ultimately, if a company is helping pay the bills, it’s hard to be truly objective about them. What I realized, however, is that it’s hard for me to be objective about Stripe anyway. 

I wanted to be a professional blogger long before I started Stratechery; however, I thought I had missed my chance, particularly as it became clear that advertising was not a long term business model for a one-person site. However, when Stripe launched with support for recurring billing, I realized there was a better model: subscriptions. 13 years later, and I’m still a happy customer. Or, to put it another way, I’m already conflicted because I love Stripe. 

 I’m not the only one: more than 5 million businesses use Stripe, accounting for 1.7% of global GDP. Moreover, a lot of those businesses are Internet native and accretive to the world’s economy, which is to say that Stripe is literally making the world a better place. That’s an easy company to get behind, especially since they have been behind Stratechery from the very beginning. — Ben Thompson

---

 Stratechery Articles and Updates

 Do You Trust Apple? — Apple has a lot of trust in terms of delivering integrated products and preserving privacy; the real trust question is if you think Siri AI will justify investing more in their ecosystem.

 Muse Spark Open, Meta + Apple, Thin and Thick — Meta has a new open source model, and to everyone’s surprise, they are are partnering with Apple to make sure you can run it locally.

 Netflix Earnings, Business or Franchise, Disney’s Deal — Netflix has a solid business, which is exactly the problem: the company increasingly seems like a business and not a franchise, at least in terms of growth.

 An Interview with Craig Moffett About SpaceX and Bubbles — An interview with Craig Moffett about SpaceX, from launch to broadband to mobile, plus how he is applying the lessons of the dot-com bubble to today.

 Sharp Text by Andrew Sharp

 You Can See Everything (And It’s a Great Time) — Nathan Fielder’s movie lives up to the hype and captures the modern world better than any art in recent memory.

blogs.name: Tomasz Tunguz
blogs.title: How Large is the AI Circle?
blogs.description: Every major technology build-out requires two phases, according to Carlota Perez1: the infrastructure to power it, & then the applications…
blogs.content:
Every major technology build-out requires two phases, according to Carlota Perez 1 : the infrastructure to power it, & then the applications to pay for it.

 Between 1996 & 2005, American telecom companies spent $1.5t building the internet in today’s dollars. 2 Meanwhile, applications riding on that infrastructure booked $180 billion of revenue. 3

 That’s an interesting ratio, isn’t it? Application revenue to infrastructure spend. It matters because the shorter the gap between the two, the sooner the infrastructure pays for itself. Let’s compare this to the AI era.

 It would take a decade for dark fiber to fill its promise, flooded with the packets of application revenue. AI is achieving that mark in half the time.

 AI hit double digits in its fourth year. Plus, the unit economics from companies like SpaceX suggest that the paybacks on the infrastructure from this revenue are short, about a year. 4

 US venture invested $516b in the first nine months of 2026. That is already 44% above the full-year record set in 2021. 5 Inflation-adjusted, the run-up in venture investment is roughly two & a half times the size of the earlier era. 6

 In a very real sense, the entire ecosystem is hoping the gap between application revenue & infrastructure investment is significantly shorter on an inflation-adjusted basis. Cumulative venture investment in this wave is about six times the first four years of the web era. 6

 The major risk is whether the ecosystem is an ouroboros: is all the spend just within startups? 7

 Ramp’s data show that 80% of the largest AI spenders are venture-backed. Those firms now account for more than 13% of American employment, up from about 5% during the web era. The circularity is real, but the circle is a sixth of the economy.

 That is a much larger circle. 8

---

 Perez, Technological Revolutions and Financial Capital , 2002. Her central mechanism is a sequence: installation of infrastructure, then financial speculation, then a turning point, then deployment of the applications that justify the spending.  ↩︎

 USTelecom historical broadband provider capex, all-in across wireline, wireless & cable. Nominal spend of $761.9b for 1996-2005, converted to 2026 dollars with CPI-U (2.116 to 1.699 across the period).  ↩︎

 A 24-company panel from SEC 10-K and S-1 filings: Amazon, Yahoo, Google, eBay, Priceline, Expedia, Travelocity, Overstock, Netflix, DoubleClick, Overture, Ask Jeeves, LookSmart, Excite, E*Trade, Ameritrade, Schwab online, Monster, CNET, WebMD, Salesforce, MSN, Hotmail and Match. The 2001-2005 figures are a floor; four companies never broke out their online revenue. Google & Yahoo are gross of traffic acquisition cost. Nominal $100.9b, converted to 2026 dollars, or about $182b; rounded in the text to $180b.  ↩︎

 SpaceX’s third-quarter S-1 states that “at current pricing, new compute deployments are generating a payback of less than a year.” Working through the figures in the GPU revenue ladder : a $46 per watt build costs $55,200 per card, and the $5.27 contract rate yields $46,165 of annual revenue against roughly $570 of cash operating cost, giving about a year at 1.21 years. At B200 spot prices it is 0.72 years. Reconciling the quote to a $46 per watt build implies an after-tax measure: at a 21% federal rate, bonus depreciation lifts first-year cash flow to $57,187 & shortens payback to 0.97 years, though that is a timing benefit rather than a cost reduction.  ↩︎

 PitchBook-NVCA Venture Monitor, Q3 2026, as of 30 September. The 2026 figure is nine months, not a full year, & is plotted unannualized. The full-year 2021 record was $357.9b. AI companies took 82.7% of 2026 deal value, the highest share in the dataset.  ↩︎

 Cumulative venture investment in 2026 dollars was $201.8b across the first four years of the web era (1996-1999) & $1.24t across the first four years of the AI era (2023-2026), a ratio of 6.2x. Measured against the web era’s entire decade ($630.3b) rather than its first four years, the same $1.24t is 2.0x. The four-year comparison is used in the text because it matches the two eras on elapsed time. Sources are NVCA/MoneyTree for 1996-2005, the NVCA 2026 Yearbook for 2023-2025, & the PitchBook-NVCA Venture Monitor for 2026, all inflated to 2026 dollars with CPI-U. The 2026 figure covers nine months, so the full-year multiple will be higher.  ↩︎   ↩︎

 Apollo’s analysis of the Ramp AI Index, published 22 October 2026, finds that 80.4% of the top 1% of AI spenders are venture-backed, against 13.1% for the median spender. Ramp separately reports that 80% of spend on OpenAI & Anthropic is driven by 1% of firms. Three caveats matter here. The chart measures dollars spent, not tokens, so it cannot support a claim about token share. Ramp’s sample is 85,000+ US businesses skewed toward tech, drawn from card & bill-pay data, & excludes free tools & personal-account shadow AI, which Ramp estimates at roughly 40% of AI application spend. And venture backing is not the same as venture dollars paying for the tokens: the chart shows the funding status of high-spending firms, not the source of the spend. Apollo is using the number to advance a circularity thesis & Ramp sells spend-management software, so both have an interest in it being vivid.  ↩︎

 Puri & Zarutskie put the employment share of venture-backed firms at roughly 4-7% across 1991-2005, using Census firm-level data; the Census Annual Business Survey and Longitudinal Business Database, as analysed by Ando (2025), put it near 13% for 2017-2021. The two estimates use different sources and slightly different definitions of venture backing, so this is a directional comparison across eras rather than a continuous series. Venture-backed firms remain about 0.64% of all US firms, so the employment share reflects their disproportionate size rather than their number.  ↩︎
